channel.itunes:author: Sean Shihao Yang

item.title: Quick Take — Statistical ranking with dynamic covariates
item.description: The Plackett-Luce model and its pairwise special case, the Bradley-Terry model, are workhorses for learning latent scores from comparison data — sports rankings, RLHF preference learning, any setting where you observe which item in a group wins. A natural extension is to let covariates shift those scores: a tennis player is older now, a product is shown in a different context. Prior work either drops individual effects entirely and models scores as pure functions of covariates, or keeps individual effects but fixes the covariates so they don't vary across comparisons. Neither is fully satisfying. This paper fills that gap.
item.itunes:author: Sean Shihao Yang

item.title: Statistical ranking with dynamic covariates
item.description: Statistical ranking models built on the Plackett–Luce framework assign each object a latent score, and the probability of any observed ranking is determined by those scores. Most prior work assumes that each object's score is fixed — the same no matter which comparison it appears in. This paper introduces a generalization where covariates attached to each object can vary across comparisons, meaning the same player or horse may carry a different covariate value in every race or match. The authors call this the PlusDC model — Plackett–Luce Supplemented with Dynamic Covariates. The paper provides conditions for when the model is identifiable, when the maximum likelihood estimator uniquely exists, an efficient algorithm to compute it, and a uniform consistency theorem with explicit convergence rates. Both synthetic experiments and applications to ATP tennis and Hong Kong horse racing show the model improving over the standard Plackett–Luce baseline.
item.itunes:author: Sean Shihao Yang

item.title: Quick Take — Boosting Data Analytics with Synthetic Volume Expansion
item.description: The question this paper addresses is whether high-fidelity synthetic data can systematically improve the accuracy of standard statistical methods — not just as a privacy tool or a data-sharing mechanism, but as a direct performance booster. This is genuinely contested territory: some prior work finds synthetic data helps, other work finds it hurts, and the field has lacked a principled framework for understanding when and why either outcome occurs.
item.itunes:author: Sean Shihao Yang

item.title: Boosting Data Analytics with Synthetic Volume Expansion
item.description: Synthetic data generation, a cornerstone of generative artificial intelligence, promises to reshape data science by addressing two persistent challenges: data scarcity and privacy. As synthetic data becomes more prevalent, a natural question arises — are the statistical methods we apply to it actually reliable? This paper investigates both sides of that question. On the effectiveness side, the authors introduce the Synthetic Data Generation for Analytics framework, which they call Syn. The framework applies statistical methods to high-fidelity synthetic data produced by generative models that have been fine-tuned on raw data using transfer learning. A central finding is the generational effect: as more synthetic data is added, accuracy tends to improve and then plateau or even worsen, pointing to the existence of a reflection point — an ideal synthetic sample size beyond which generation errors begin to dominate. Three case studies validate the framework across sentiment analysis, predictive modeling of structured data, and statistical inference on tabular data. On the privacy side, synthetic data imposes lower risk than raw data while remaining compatible with the differential privacy standard.
item.itunes:author: Sean Shihao Yang

item.title: Quick Take — Boosting Data Analytics with Synthetic Volume Expansion
item.description: The central question this paper addresses is whether high-fidelity synthetic data — generated by modern generative models like diffusion models — can actually improve statistical methods that were designed to run on real data. This sounds almost paradoxical: why would training on fake data help? The field has had mixed evidence on this, and this paper proposes a unified framework to understand when and how it works.
item.itunes:author: Sean Shihao Yang

item.title: Boosting Data Analytics with Synthetic Volume Expansion
item.description: Synthetic data generation has become a cornerstone of modern data science, promising a way to address both data scarcity and privacy concerns simultaneously. This paper asks a precise question: can high-fidelity synthetic data actually make statistical methods more accurate — and if so, how much synthetic data should you use?
item.itunes:author: Sean Shihao Yang

item.title: Quick Take — Predicting the impact of treatments over time with uncertainty aware neural differential equations
item.description: The core problem in treatment effect estimation from observational data is confounding: patients who receive a treatment tend to be systematically different from those who don't, so comparing outcomes directly gives biased estimates. Most methods that try to correct for this require an assumption called positive overlap — that for any patient history, both treated and untreated outcomes are actually observed somewhere in the data. In practice this assumption is hard to verify and frequently violated. This paper takes a different angle: rather than trying harder to satisfy the overlap assumption, accept that it may fail and build a model that knows when it doesn't know.
item.itunes:author: Sean Shihao Yang

item.title: Predicting the impact of treatments over time with uncertainty aware neural differential equations
item.description: Predicting the impact of treatments from observational data is a major unsolved challenge despite significant recent advances in time series modeling. When clinicians decide who receives a treatment, their decisions are typically correlated with the very features that predict outcomes — a patient's blood pressure, disease trajectory, overall prognosis. This confounding means that the population of treated patients looks systematically different from the untreated population, creating a distribution shift between what we observe and what we want to predict. Prior work on addressing this usually assumes a positive level of statistical overlap between treated and untreated groups, but overlap is both difficult to verify and rarely satisfied in practice.
item.itunes:author: Sean Shihao Yang

item.title: Green Shielding: A Framework for User-Level Query Variation in Medical AI
item.description: The central problem this paper addresses is deceptively simple: large language models behave differently depending on how you ask them things. Not adversarially — not jailbreaks or prompt injections — but in the ordinary, routine ways that real users happen to phrase their questions. A patient who writes a worried, first-person message gets a different medical response than one who writes a calm, third-person clinical description of the same condition. The authors call their framework for studying this Green Shielding, and they instantiate it in the domain of medical diagnosis.
item.itunes:author: Sean Shihao Yang

item.title: LLM-JEPA: Large Language Models Meet Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures
item.description: There is a long-standing divide at the heart of representation learning. On one side you have generative methods, which learn by reconstructing their inputs — predicting the next token, filling in masked patches, or decoding a compressed representation back to pixel space. On the other side you have Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures, or JEPAs, which instead operate entirely in embedding space: they learn by predicting the embedding of one view of an input from the embedding of another view, with no attempt to reconstruct the original. In vision, this distinction has turned out to matter enormously. JEPA-style objectives consistently outperform reconstruction objectives on perception and knowledge-discovery tasks, partly because they escape the biases introduced by operating in raw input space — the kind of fine-grained pixel-level detail that is irrelevant to understanding a scene.
item.itunes:author: Sean Shihao Yang
